speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Certainly, these contractors' accounts, $8,000,000 in one case and $6,000,000 in the other, had not been included in the $41,000,000 above.

But from the $100,000,000 it is stated that $14,000,000 is deducted, leaving for construction $100,000,000, less $14,000,000, or about $86,000,000. The Solicitor General says:	I cannot explain it to-day, but I will do it later on.

I am fortunate again in being able to assure the right hon. gentleman that the explanation I gave is the correct one. I have consulted with the auditor since, and he has confirmed what I stated supplemented by what my right hon. friend the Prime Minister has said. The $21,262,000 is the amount owing on construction as of the 31st of December. That all does not appear in the $14,954,714, but that $14,954,714 is as it is said to be on the very face of the return, ' sub-contractors ' accounts not in above.' In the ' above requirements to complete ' are

included some of the sub-contractors' accounts. The $41,987,565 and the $27,441,086 include the balance of the amount of $21,-
262,000	not included in the item of $14,954,714.

Does not the Solicitor
General consider it would have been a great deal better if all of the sub-contractors' accounts had been included in the same item, so that we would have known where we were at?

It might have been -clearer, but the information is all here; there is nothing left out. There are some contractors' peculiarities of accounting that I am not any more familiar with than is the *hon. gentleman.
Mr. PUGSLEY; Does the Solicitor General assure the committee that the difference between the $14,000,000 and the $21,000,000 he speaks of is not due to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, as the principal contractors?

They are not, in the ordinary sense, contractors at all. They simply act as a construction department of the road. They are contractors in the sense that they incur contractors' obligations, raise money during construction, pending returns from subsidies and proceeds of bonds; but they are not contractors in the sense that they themselves contract with the Canadian Northern railway, by any written documents or by any understanding, to do the work at a fixed price. They simply get the work done as cheaply and as well as possible, and the Canadian Northern railway pays the accounts.

How do they get that
stock issued as fully paid up if they do not get the work done as contractors?

The hon. gentleman would scarcely deny that if they did no more than I have named in my second last sentence, that is raise the money, themselves becoming responsible and financing $244,000,000 of construction, they would be entitled to some remuneration for that? If paid in stock, depending on the success of the enterprise, would they not be entitled to some very considerable remuneration? I do not know what percentage the hon. gentleman would think fair.

I am sure that the hon. gentleman would not attempt to assure the committee that Messrs. Mackenzie and

Mann have not become very wealthy out of this railroad construction.

If the hon. gentleman will read the return he will see that the Government auditors an whom he has confidence and has, through years, expressed and preserved his confidence, have reported that on this construction Mackenzie, Mann and Company have not made anything except the common stock that they have, and that common stock represents a great deal more than merely their services as construction agents for the Canadian Northern railway.

Do they report what
the assets of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, are worth?
No, they do not. Is the hon. gentleman very anxious to find out?

Not at all. I think myself that if Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, are worth a great many millions of dollars, as reported, it would not be unreasonable, as they are really in truth and in fact the Canadian Northern Railway Company, that they should put up those assets as a security to the people of this country for their guarantee of this enormous amount of $45,000,000.
Why did you not have them put it up when you gave them a subsidy?

It is a very different
proposition to-day; they are coming now in a very different position, they are asking us, in addition to making them a present last year of the enormous sum of $15,000,000, to give them a guarantee or endorsement of $45,000,000 more. If it is true, as I say it is, and as the people of this country know it is, that Messrs. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, are the Canadian Northern Railway Company, that they are the same persons under a different corporate name, they own all the stock of the Canadian Northern railway, they are the Canadian Northern railway.
They will not be if you allow this Bill to pass.

Well they will be partners at all events, they will be the controlling partner and, more than that, they will be able to go to the financial people in the old world and say: the Government is our junior partner, it owns $40,000,000 of the paid-up stock and it cannot see us go down; it will have to stand at our

backs and make this stock valuable, and you will be perfectly safe in investing in this common stock. What I say is that tdie Government seem to have thought it important to ascertain how much profit Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann, Company, Limited, have made out of construction. Why did they not go a little farther and find out what were their assets, because their assets would be accumulated either out of construction or out of financial operations in connection with the Canadian Northern railway; and money could be made out of financing hundreds of millions of securities for the Canadian Northern railway just as well as out of construction. Does my hon. friend see that? I do think, if they are in reality the Canadian Northern railway as everybody knows they are, it would be reasonable that these assets should be put up as a security for the obligation which the people of Canada are assuming.
Mr. ME1GHEN: The hon. gentleman says that our investigation into their Profits 0 construction was not sufficient, tha we should have investigated whether or not they made any money by way of rake-o on the sale of securities.
I did not use the word rake-off. I said profit from financing.

Profit from financing; it may be more euphonious but it means the same thing. We now know that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, did act as construction agents of the Canadian Northern railway. Therefore, we felt it was our duty to see whether they had in any way absorbed these moneys that- .should have gone into the railroad. We did not know and do not know now that they acted as agents for the sale of the bonds of the 'Canadian Northern railway.
Did not the hon. member a few moments ago, say that they had done financing for the Canadian Northern railway?
They did incur financial obligations, raising money for the purpose of building the road.
Yes, out of bonds guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada, by the province of British Columbia, by the province of Manitoba, by the province of Saskatchewan and by the province of Nova Scotia.
Not at all.
Is it not just as important-
They did not do that.
Oh, yes.
No, they did not.
Is my hon. friend sure of that ?
Sure, yes.
Does he suggest that they raised the money without security ?

They raised it on their
own assets.
Mackenzie and Mann; and what do their assets consist of ?
That is not our business.

Does not my hon. friend see that if it is important to ascertain how much money Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, have made out of construction, it is equally important to see how much money they made out of the Canadian Northern railway by financing for them and selling their bonds, selling the various securities which were guaranteed by the Governments of Canada and of the various provinces? They may have made millions out of this, and it would detract just as much from the resources of the Canadian Northern railway as if they had made it out of construction.

The hon. gentleman is wrong at both ends; I shall start, though, with the end he was at first. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, financed the construction of the road; but they financed it not out of funds the proceeds of securities guaranteed by the Dominion or by anybody else; they financed it on their own resources in so far as their operations were concerned. They raised the money in advance of receipt of these securities, and they raised it on their own resources. Then as the proceeds came in they were recouped the moneys they paid out. For a gentleman having such a knowledge of railroad construction as the hon. member for St. John, I am surprised that my hon. friend does not appreciate the fact that construction has to go on and be done as far as it goes before a dollar of proceeds of guaranteed securities can be obtained. How is the money to be raised to do that ? Somebody has to do it. Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann put up the money for the Canadian Northern railway. They were afterwards recouped out of the proceeds of the

bond guarantee and of other bonds to a total of some $323,000,000, but they have expended some $224,000,000, leaving $21,000,000 owing to those who did work for which Messrs. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, have never received money from the Canadian Northern railway to pay. We knew that they had that association with the road and we made it our business to investigate. We rose to a sense of duty w'hich the hon. gentleman never rose to when he came to the assistance of the Canadian Northern railway or by Mackenzie and Mann.
You rose to a sense of only half duty.

Better half duty than
none at all. But we did not know, and we do not know yet that, in the sale of Canadian Northern bonds, Mackenzie, Mann and Company acted in any capacity whatever. My information is that they did not; that the Canadian Northern sold their own bonds, and that the auditors of this Government have traced the whole proceeds of those bonds right into the road itself. I am surprised' that, when Mackenzie, Mann and Company, under the guise of the Canadian Northern Ontario, came to the hon. member for St, John in 1911 and said:	We cannot build the Canadian Northern Ontario unless you come to our aid; you will have to do something for us as the Government of Canada; we cannot do it without your help, that my hon. friend did not say: Where are your stocks, your other assets, that you did not make out of the Canadian Northern at all, that you made in speculations elsewhere? Put that down before we give you a dollar's worth of bond guarantee from this Government. That is what my hon. friend should have done, seeing that he takes this position now. As long as Mackenzie, Mann and Company do not absorb out of the Canadian Northern Railway Company anything that is intended to go into the assets of that company, we have not any business with Mackenzie, Mann and Company. But inasmuch as the townsite company derived value from the fact that the Canadian Northern railway itself went through where the townsites are or into their neighbourhood, we felt that they should put that in as security, and they have done so. Those are their own assets according to law. They have placed in security $10,000,000 worth of stock and $10,000,000 worth of bonds against the guarantee of this Government. That is something the hon. gentleman never thought

of before when he was giving a guarantee in 1911, or was giving subsidies many years before.
He was not taking third mortgages.

As the townsite company derived value from that fact, and because of the fact that it was available, we felt that it was not asking too much that they should pledge that as their security. We have discussed all this; we have gone by all this position, and I do not think I ought to delay the committee and I do not think the hon. member for St. John ought to delay the committee in discussing something that has been discussed threadbare already.

I am very sorry indeed if I am delaying the committee. I would not like to have my hon. friend think that I am seeking to do so. It was my misfortune that I was not able to hear the discussion; and if, by reason of that, I am dealing with something that has already been thrashed out, I trust that the committee will pardon me; but I think that my hon. friend is not doing justice to himself in seeking to make the committee believe that the position of affairs to-day is the same as it was when the previous Government guaranteed the bonds. At that time, the Canadian Northern had a good financial standing.
Why did you not make them go to the markets and get the money?
What that Government did was to guarantee first mortgage bonds.
Why did they come to you at all?
Because, by reason of having the Government guarantee, they would be able to get the money a little cheaper.
Was that the explanation you gave at the time?

But they come to the Government to-day and say: If you do not come to our assistance, we shall have to go into bankruptcy. They are in an unfortunate position. I suppose perhaps that this position may result somewhat from the terrible depression which has spread' over the country west during the last two years.

If they only came for their own advantage to get money a little cheaper, where is the difference? Why did

not the hon. gentleman say to them: You have lots of assets of your own; put them in; get the money more cheaply that way; why do you come to us? Is not the point just the same, no matter in what capacity they come?
I claim that the company is in a very different position to-day in respect to this $45,000,000 from what it was in in respect to the guarantee which they asked for from the previous Government.
You do not answer the question.

They came then with a good security-a first mortgage. They were proposing to link up the system so as to connect Montreal w'ith the base of the Rocky mountains. There "was evidence that it would be an exceedingly good system, and that it would be a safe proposition to guarantee the first mortgage bonds. To-day they are coming to the Government and they say: Every bit of 'property which we have is mortgaged; we cannot raise any more money on it in the markets of the world, and, unless the Government comes to our assistance, we shall be obliged to go under. In these circumstances, the Government has felt it to be its duty to find out whether Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, have made any money out of the construction of the railway; but, knowing, as they must, as the whole country knows, that Mackenzie, Mann and Company have assets of enormous value, they do not go into the whole matter; knowing as they do that Mackenzie, Mann and Company financed for the Canadian Northern'-financed for themselves under the name of the Canadian Northern -they do not seek, through their auditors, to ascertain what money Mackenzie, Mann and Company made out of the financing, out of the commissions, but they simply limit their auditors to find out what they made out of the construction of the railway. iSurely, if there were $10,000,000 worth of bonds which Mackenzie, Mann and Company financed, and for which they only turned into the Canadian Northern 80 per cent-
They turned in all. The auditors so found.
I have not seen any report to that effect.
Then, you have not read it.
I have not seen any report that they have turned in the par value of the bonds.

They did not sell at
par.
Does the hon. gentleman pretend to say that the securities guaranteed by the Dominion and the different provinces and sold four or five years ago, did not sell at par?

Wherever they sold at par or above par the whole proceeds are traced by our auditors and found to be planted in the road. The auditors traced the full amount at which the bonds sold and followed it into the road itself.

Where is the report of
that?
It is on the table.
Then, why is it that my hon. friend cannot say whether or not Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, charged commission to the Canadian Northern railway?
I know they did not because they did not act as agents on the sale.
Does he say that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, got no profit either out of financing for the Canadian Northern railway or out of construction?
I am able to assure the House of that on the authority of the auditors of this Government.

I will accept that assurance of my hon. friend if he knows it. But I will say that it is entirely contrary to my own information. Not very long ago I had information from a very high financial authority, an officer of a financial institution who would be in a position to speak as to the circumstances that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, were rich beyond the dreams of avarice. They have been connected entirely with the construction ot roads belonging to the Canadian Northern Railway system. I would like to ask, then, how they made this enormous wealth unless it was out of railway construction or out of financing for the Canadian Northern railway?

One other thing. The hon. gentleman says that roads must be constructed before the bonds are issued. I defy him to point to a single road of importance constructed by the Canadian Northern railway for which there was not legislation providing either for subsidies or for the guarantee of bonds before a single mile of the road was constructed. And when Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, or Sir William Mackenzie or Sir Donald Mann would go to the financiers of the world they would be able to point to legislation providing for the guarantee of the bonds; and I venture to say that not a dollar would be advanced by the financiers except by the bonds being pledged to be delivered over to them when actually issued under the authority of Parliament or the legislature of the province concerned.
I am not making objection now to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, making millions-if they did make them- out of financing the road. What I am arguing is that the position of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, is practically the same as if it were the Canadian Northern Railway Company that had in its vaults the assets that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, have. So far as their assets are concerned, as I have said, they are in effect the Canadian Northern railway. Now, why should not they put up their assets? If through the action of the Government this undertaking is pulled through, they stand to make. If the stock which the Government is taking is worth anything-and hon. gentlemen are trying to make the country believe that it is a most valuable asset, or may be in the future -Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, will have $60,000,000 with the stock at par. If it becomes worth only fifty cents on the dollar they stand to make $30,000,000. Why, then, should not they stand behind the Government to the extent of their assets? Can the Government make any answer to that? If Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, were not really the Canadian Northern railway, if they did not hold this stock of the company there would be no point to my argument. But they hold all the stock except the $7,000,000 given over to the Government last year. But the Government is going to pledge the credit of the people to this enormous amount as a result of which these gentlemen, if the operation proves successful, will be immensely rich, yet nothing of theirs is pledged. The Government auditors were

void: Do not look into the assets of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, but only report whether they made money out of construction; as to what they are worth, as to the stocks they have in their treasury, be careful not to report to Parliament or give information on that subject.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Government gave no such instructions, but gave instructions to inquire whether every dollar derived from the proceeds of these securities had gone into the road or was available in the bank. The auditors have reported accordingly that that was the case. The hon. gentleman is speaking absolutely without warrant, and must know it, when he assumes that the Government gave any such instructions as those to which he has alluded. He is taking the point that the assets of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, derived altogether from ventures outside of this railway, should be brought in. I would ask him a question:	Did he consider the securities which he guaranteed as a member of the late Administration of 1911 marketable without the guarantee of the Government?

The first mortgage
bonds? I say, frankly, the matter was not in my department, and I gave no thought to the question.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The difference between
the late Administration and this is just there-we did give thought to the question. The hon. member has not been in his place during the debate, and therefore did not hear the observations of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), who stated that the mere fact that these securities were brought here and the Government was asked to endorse them was an indication that they could not be saleable without that guarantee, and therefore the security they afforded was absolutely inadequate. I do not think I am misstating his argument. Precisely the same argument applied to the securities which were guaranteed in 1911, would lead to the conclusion that the security then offered was also valueless. Whether that be the case or not, I think it can be demonstrated to the satisfaction of any reasonable man that the security offered in respect to this guarantee is a better security than that which the late Government took in 1911 in respect of the Canadian Northern Ontario.
That is, the right hon. gentleman believes that a second mortgage is better than a first.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I do not think a second mortgage is better than a first. But I think that a first mortgage of $35,000 a mile upon a particular piece of line may be a more dangerous risk to the country than a third mortgage if the prior charges together with the charge created by the third mortgage amount to the same sum and are secured upon a very much better piece of line; thus, I think that my right hon. friend from St. John-
Not ' right hon.'

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am glad to have referred to the hon. gentleman in that way, and trust it may be only a presage of what may come in the future. We will not quarrel about that. Now, the security which the late Government guaranteed in 1911 was $35,000 a mile upon the Canadian Northern Ontario, and according to the hon. member for South Renfrew, that security could not be regarded as marketable without the guarantee of the Government. The hon. member for St. John has not controverted that statement, but said that he had not given thought or consideration to that question. But assuming that he had given thought and consideration to it, I assume he would have insisted on Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, at that time utilizing these enormous private resources to which he has alluded. Would he deny that?

If on consideration I had thought the security was not a good one, I should have insisted that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, should put up their private resources. I think that would be reasonable. As I have said, that was a first mortgage, and this is a third mortgage, I understand.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Taking the hon. gentleman's contention, it is a great pity that he had not begun thinking of this matter three years ago instead of now, because if he had done so then, according to his present statement, the country would have had security which he thinks now should have been brought in.
It is not too late.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is not too late, if it is necessary or desirable, or if any good reason could be put forward for it. But we
do not attach great importance to arguments of that kind put forward by hon. gentlemen opposite who did not regard the matter as worthy of thought when they had to deal with it. Therefore, we must be guided largely by our own views in that respect, because it is rather late in the day for my hon. friend to awaken to a necessity upon which, according to his statement, he did not bestow any consideration three years ago.

My right hon. friend's remarks in regard to his own conduct in this respect justify the argument of the hon. member for the city of St. John. The hon. gentleman said that in 1911 we took a first mortgage upon the line of railway which was subsidized, that is to say, from Port Arthur to Montreal. At that time the company were in good standing and we thought that the subsidies then given would enable them to finance the enterprise. When my right hon. friend came into office, the same company came to him for assistance, as they had come to us, and he gave a guarantee upon the line from St. Albert to the boundary of British Columbia to the extent of $35,000 a mile, taking a first mortgage upon the road, just as we had done. The reasons for giving assistance in 1912 were the same as they were in 1911, but everybody supposed, and rightly so, that the assistance which was then given would be sufficient to carry on the enterprise. My hon. friend says that conditions have altered and that the company says to the Government: We are in poor standing to-day; we are not in as good standing as we were in 1911; we cannot raise any money on our own securities and can do no more than we have done. Therefore we come to you; you are the only recourse we have to enable us to carry the enterprise to a conclusion. My hon. friend says: You cannot deal with this matter as dt was dealt with in 1911 and in 1912; the conditions are such that the promoters of this enterprise should be asked to give much more than was given formerly. Formerly, he says, we were content to take a mortgage upon the enterprise and the resources of the company; now, we should go beyond that and take in also the resources of the individual promoters. What objection has my hon. friend the Solicitor General to that? He says that Mackenzie and Mann never got a dollar out of this enterprise. Nobody is supposed to work for nothing in this world; everybody for his work is entitled to a legitimate remuneration, but my hon. friend says that
4UIH

these men who, in carrying on this work would be supposed to have human motives, were working for philanthropy and that they have gained nothing at all through the carrying on of this enterprise.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My right hon. friend alludes to what was done in 1912. It may be that at that time we had in view the bad example which has been offered to us by hon. gentlemen on the other side, but as soon as we had time for reflection we brought about a very different order of things. My right hon. friend, endeavouring to be sarcastic, alludes to these gentlemen as philanthropists. I do not think that anything of that kind was suggested by hon. gentlemen on this side. I suppose that Mackenzie and Mann went into the business of constructing railways in the first instance for the purpose of making a fortune for themselves, but I do believe that afterwards they got the idea of bringing about the consummation of a great transcontinental railway, and it seems to me that some of the instances which have been alluded to show that they were content to put aside for a moment the gains which might have been theirs and to put certain assets which they might properly have claimed under the laws of the road into the project of constructing this national transcontinental railway. I do not think that they were philanthropists; I do think that they were animated by a desire to make money; but they were animated also by a desire to bring about the construction of a third transcontinental railway. I am willing to concede that they are quite as selfish as the ordinary run of humanity; perhaps they may be more so; I do not know about that. But under the legislation carried out under the administration of hon. gentlemen opposite, partly in this Parliament and partly in provincial legislatures, but largely in this Parliament, it was possible for these men not only to secure as their own the common stock about which so much has been said in this debate, but also so to carry on their affairs that, in addition to that they would have a claim against the Canadian Northern railway and the allied companies for many millions of. dollars. Perhaps $20,000,000 or $25,000,000, and that claim, in the event of the success of this road, would have 'been a collectable claim. I say that my right hon. friend did not take the pains in 1911 or at any other time to investigate the affairs of the Canadian Northern RailfSir Wilfrid Laurier.]
way Company and its allied companies for the purpose of ascertaining these conditions and that therefore, when they gave this guarantee the conditions may be described in this way:	In the first place, according
to the assertion of the hon. member for St. John city, they did not give even any thought or consideration to bringing in any of these assets about which so much has been said in this debate. In the second place, they did not investigate the affairs of the Canadian Northern railway for the purpose of determining whether it could be successfully carried through as a national enterprise; they took the word of the promoters for it. In the third place, they did not investigate the affairs of the company for the purpose of determining whether or not the promoters had made any profits out of construction; they did not think that was worth while. In the fourth place, they did not make any such investigation as was necessary for the purpose of ascertaining that in addition to the common stock there was on the part of Mackenzie and Mann, iLimited, that enormous claim involving perhaps $25,000,000. We did not go about this business in that way. We sent on two occasions the best men that we could find in the service of the Government for the purpose of making a thorough inquiry into all such matters as they could usefully investigate. Of course, they could not investigate the ultimate cost of the construction of the road, as they were not experts in that regard. They satisfied us that in addition to the common stock held by Mackenzie and Mann there was this claim impending against the Canadian Northern railway and its allied companies of many millions of dollars. What did we do in that regard? We said, in the first place: You must put into this security all assets of the Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited, in so fair as they have relation to the carrying out of this enterprise; for example, the townsite properties. In the second place, we said: You must take care of that floating indebtedness amounting to $8,000,000, in excess of what it ought to be. In the third place, we said: You, Mackenzie and Mann, must take care of these temporary loans in so far as they will not be taken care of by the securities which have been pledged against them. In the fourth place, we said: You, Mackenzie and Mann, have very large holdings of common stock in this company and you have very large claims which may amount

to many millions of dollars against this company; we require you, if the country is to come to your assistance at the present juncture, in the first place, to hand over two-fifths of that stock in order that this country, if the enterprise is canned to a successful conclusion, shall participate in [DOT]some reasonable way in the advantages which result from the aid now afforded. And, further, we said: Inasmuch as you have a claim, which might be asserted in the future, to the extent of $20,000,000 or $25,000,000 against the Canadian Northern and its allied companies, we are requiring you, Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and you, Sir William Mackenzie and Sir Donald Mann, to absolutely release every ddllar of that claim, and it must be released before you get one dollar of the proceeds of these securities. Under these circumstances, if hon. gentlemen desire to contrast the course taken by the late Administration in 1911 with the course taken by the Administration of to-day, I am perfectly happy and willing and contented that they should do so.
Sir WilLFRID LAURIER: I will venture to contrast the attitude of the two Governments in regard to the Canadian Northern railway, and I am pleased to do it. My right hon. friend is taking precautions now, when the company is in a state of collapse, but he did not take any such precautions in 1912, when the company was in a good financial condition. When the company came to him in 1912 he assisted them by a guarantee of $35,000 a mile on the 116 miles from St. Albeit to the Rocky mountains, but he took no security at all. He never held an investigation into their books, nor did he inquire into the financial condition of the company. The following year they came again to Parliament for assistance, and what did my right hon. friend do? Did he ascertain their financial condition by an accounting? Far from it. In the year 1912 he had come to the assistance of the company to the extent of a guarantee of $35,000 a mile on the 116 miles from St. Albert to the Rocky mountains, and in the following year, 1913, he gave to the railway running through that very same territory a cash subsidy of $12,000 a mile without a word about any security. It was simply taking money from the treasury and giving it to Mackenzie and Mann. Not content with that, we had given assistance by guaranteeing the bonds of the company to the
extent of $35,000 a mile for the road between Port Arthur and Montreal. They came again last year, and, after they had already been granted a guarantee of their bonds, my right hon. friend gave them a cash subsidy of $12,000 a mile. So that last year my hon. friend gave to that same company, without any inquiry into their books, and without any investigation, a cash subsidy of $14,000,000. And what did he get for it? $7,000,000 of watered stock. That is the financing of my right hon. friend, and I am happy to contrast his system with ours.

I think my right hon. friend has overlooked another point. It was not until last year that the claims of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, against the Canadian Northern were important enough to be considered. Then for the first time the Government began to deal in the common stock of the Canadian Northern railway. My right hon. friend knows that any debts of the Canadian Northern to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, would come ahead of common stock. When the late G^ernment aided the Canadian Northern by a guarantee of bonds, it was simply guaranteeing something which stood ahead of claims of every kind and description.

The hon. gentleman
means that even if Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, had robbed the road, we would still assist them?
There is no suggestion that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, have robbed the road except from my hon. friend. He is the first one to suggest such a thing.

We are glad of that
assurance.

Surely it is not necessary for me to repeat that any claim of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, while it would stand ahead of the $7,000,000 of stock which the Government took last year and of the $45,000,000 now proposed, it would not stand ahead of the first mortgage debentures which the Government guaranteed when my right hon. leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) was in office. Therefore, it did not become necessary to look into the claims of the Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, on the Canadian Northern, because the security which the Government was guaranteeing would stand ahead of any claims of that character.

Does not ours stand
ahead of it?
No, your $40,000,000 of stock would not stand ahead of their claims.

That is not our security. Our security is the guaranteed securities that are given to secure the $45,000,000 Does that not stand ahead of the claims of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, the same as yours did?

My hon. friend knows
perfectly well that to-day that security is not worth a snap of the finger.
I do not know, and if my hon. friend has an open mind I will be able to show him that dollar for dollar our security is worth twice, and more, the money they are getting.

I can assure my hon.
friend that I have a very open mind.
At six o'clock, the Committee took recess.
The Committee resumed at eight o'clock, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
I did not say that.

I think that is what was stated-that the auditors were instructed to look into the question of what assets Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited, had derived from the construction of lines of railways or from financing the different systems.
To look into the disposition of all the moneys raised on the securities of the road or raised in any way.

That, in effect, is telling the auditors to make no report with regard to the other assets, or as to the wealth of Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited. Therefore the Government are not prepared to give to the House any information as to whether the report is true that Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited, are possessed of very large wealth, indeed, enormous wealth, because that is the rumour. It has been argued on this side of the House, and it can be argued with the greatest confidence before the people, that before we are committed to this enormous liability Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann Company should put up their assets behind the guarantee as a further security for the guarantee which the Government is to be called upon to give. The Solicitor General made a statement that for a reason which he thought satisfactory Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited, were called upon to put up the security of townsites. Would my hon. friend be good enough to tell me what these are?

It would take a long time. They represent a great many assets, all the townsites acquired in connection with the lines in western Canada by Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann Company, Limited, and all the agreements of sale and sums realized thereon.
Can the Solicitor General tell me in the name of what company these are held?
The Canadian Northern Town Properties, Limited.
Does that include the most valuable of all, the townsite at Montreal?
I do not understand that Messrs. Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, own the site at Montreal.
Who does own it?
I have no information to give the House on that point.

I may say that I do
not think the Solicitor General ought to shut his eyes to knowledge which everybody else has.
I do not shut my eyes.

The Canadian Northern Railway townsite, which is upon the northern side of Mount Royal, was stated by the newspapers at the time to have been acquired by the Canadian Northern Railway Company or Mackenzie and Mann. It was handled by their officials, by the firm of Davidson, McRae and Company, who handle all the land of the Canadian Northern railway, and was recognized and known by everybody to be the Canadian Northern Railway townsite. I venture to say that town-site is worth more than all the other town-sites of the Canadian Northern railway put together, that is a townsite from which they will derive millions of dollars.

If the hon. gentleman
will show to the House that they own the townsite, I will undertake, on behalf of the Government, that it will be put in.

It is not for members
on this side of the House to show that. Let me ask my hon. friend if he has made inquiry as to who bought the land for that townsite, who laid it out, who placed it on the market. Has he made inquiry as to that? If he has not I may tell him that the land was acquired by the gentlemen who do the land business for the Canadian Northern Railway Company. It was laid out by their engineers, it was put upon the market by their agents, and it is known to the people of Montreal to be the townsite of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. I do not care under what name they have actually handled it, whether it is the Canadian Northern Townsite Company-
Under any name at all.
Or the Canadian Northern Land Company.
Show that they own it in any way whatever.
Have you asked them?

It is another evidence
that the Solicitor General has taken whatever that eminent lawyer Mr. Lash, who received that commendation, from the Fin-
ance Minister, has chosen to give to him and he has been very careful to pick out a vast number of properties of comparatively little value and to retain to these gentlemen the properties which are of very great value.

What does the hon.
gentleman consider comparatively little value?

I would regard most of these townsites; as of very little value as compared with the townsite at Montreal which has been excepted from the securities handed over to the Government as a further security for the guarantee which they are called upon to enter into. I feel that in entering into this guarantee and entering into this liability the Government has certainly not proceeded with that reasonable caution which they should have adopted. I believe that they ought to have taken every security. I do not think they are entitled to any great credit for doing what they have done. They have received a good deal of praise in the Government press, and I understand that they gave themselves a good deal of praise and credit for what is said to be the very able way in which the Solicitor General has safeguarded the interests of the Dominion. What, Sir, has he done? He has simply drafted here a resolution which provides that the equity in these different properties which form a part of the Canadian Northern Railway system shall be handed over to the Government as a security for the guarantee of this $45,000, 000. I do not think that is such a wonderful feat, and more particularly would I hesitate to call it a wonderful feat when I find that some, at all events, of the very best securities which could have been given, those of the very greatest value, have been excepted from the securities which have been given to the Government.

In the few remarks I made to the House the other evening, I spoke regarding the Halifax and Southwestern railway. My information is that this railway collects all the freight and passenger rates to which it is entitled, but that it has failed to pay anything for the use of the terminal facilities of the Intercolonial at Halifax. I am speaking only from information given to me, and I cannot absolutely assert what I am saying. My information, however, is that this has been going on for many years, and that, in consequence, there is a very large deficit, and that the Halifax and Southwestern railway owes the Intercolonial railway a very large

amount of money, which in some way has been transposed on the books of the company so as not to show a deficit. I should like the Solicitor General to let me know in what position the Halifax and Southwestern railway stands in regard to the amount which it owes for the use of the terminal facilities of the Intercolonial at Halifax.
The other night I endeavoured to lay what stress I could on the fact that the personal securities of Mackenzie and Mann had not been put up so ias to show the faith they had in this enterprise, for which they are at present endeavouring to get $45,000,000 from the people of this country. As I stated the other night, I understand that, besides railways, they own the Dunsmuir coal mines, large timber areas in British Columbia, and large fishing interests, from which, I am told, they have, either this year or the year before, received dividends to the extent of 60 per cent. I thoroughly believe in all that the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) has said, namely, that you may call them Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, you may call them Mackenzie, Mann and Company, you may say Canadian Northern, but when you come down to the last analysis, the concern is William Mackenzie and Donald Mann. Therefore, when these men ask this enormous sum from this Parliament and this country, taking into consideration all that they have received already from this country, if they have personal securities, I want to put it as forcibly as I can that these men should be asked to show the faith that they have in their own enterprise, in the enterprise that the people of Canada have built from start to finish until to-day they have hundreds of millions of dollars invested in it, by putting these personal securities into this enterprise. It is not the duty of the Government to say: We shall ask them to do this, if you can show us so and so and so and so. The Government are here, whether they like it or not, as trustees for the people of Canada. The hon, member for St. John has pointed out that Mackenzie and Mann own the Model City at Montreal, which they have exploited; and every one in the Dominion knows that Mackenzie and Mann -I do not care what name you call them- have made millions of dollars out of that investment. If the Government are put on their guard and are told, as they have been told, that Mackenzie and Mann own this Model City, the duty of the Government, as 257
trustees for the people of Canada, is to protect the people by seeing that these assets are put in this agreement. As the Government have been put on their guard, from the speeches made in this House and from the information given them, I ask why these personal assets of Mackenzie and Mann are 'eft out, and why Mackenzie and Mann are allowed to saddle this huge burden on to the people of Canada, seeing that they themselves are allowed, by reason of limited companies, with their stocks paid up and no further liabilities against them, to go free. I have little to say in regard to these limited companies, except that the paid-up stock has been paid up in a most remarkable manner. Again, I ask, why it is that the Government of the Dominion of Canada, having had due notice of what Mackenzie and Mann's interests are in a personal way, should not, instead of saying to the Opposition, show me, themselves say, we have had notice, and, if Mackenzie and Mann, or Mackenzie and Mann. Limited, own these securities, then we shall see that, for the protection of the people of Canada, these securities are put into this agreement.

The hon. member for
West Lambton asks if we have any information as to a rumour which he has heard that there is an outstanding account against the Halifax and Southwestern railway for the use of the Intercolonial railway. I know of no such account. All I know in that relation is that, on the statement of floating liabilities of the company, there appears an item of $191,261.16, as attributable to the Halifax and Southwest-lern railway. That is their share of the floating liabilities. Beyond that I can give no further information.

Is that unpaid interest
on bonds?

No, it is current liabilities. For the information of the hon. gentleman, or rather that he may not be turned aside from the truth by the very reckless statements that have been made in this House, there is no unpaid interest on bonds in any of these companies. There is no receivership due either to-night or at any other time. The interest on all the bonds has been paid, and is being paid right along.
The rest of the discourse of the hon. member for West Lambton was largely on the same old subject; and, mindful of the fact that explanations made heretofore

407u

seem to have been of no avail, but simply bring back the same retorts with a little more emphasis when they come from the iron, member for West Lambton, I do not think 1 would be justified in traversing the same old ground again. The hon. member, however, towards the end of his remarks, said that in view of the fact that stock had been allotted as paid up was in reality not paid up at all, we should have lassoed under the mortgage the private assets of Mackenzie and Mann, if they had not been lassoed before. Is the hon. gentleman Teally himself convinced that the stock of the Canadian Northern, as originally allotted to Mackenzie, Mann and Company, was not honestly paid up?
How could that be?

When two men own every dollar of the common stock of a railway, a thing almost unknown in the railway world, can the hon. member tell the country and this House that these men are in the first place entitled to a large amount of money in commission for financing their own proposition?
And does he further wish to say-he may say it, but I wish to tell him the people of the country will not believe it-that these people were to receive large land grants for the building of the road, but that the proceeds of those land grants should not belong to the Canadian Northern railway and the proceeds of them should not go into the road ?
I would suggest that the hon.. member fight that out with the hon. member for St. John.

I would rather fight it out with the Solicitor General. The Solicitor General says that no one knows whether they have paid for the stock or not. Everybody knows that they have $70,000,000 of the stock of the Canadian Northern railway which is to be reduced to $60,000,000. But the hon. gentleman in his own blue-book shows that Mackenzie and Mann paid nothing for that stock. For they paid, or agreed to pay, $244,670,168 on the construction and equipment of this road. They have received in subsidies from the Dominion Government, from provincial governments, municipalities, securities and guaranteed securities, $223,407,641, leaving a balance due of $21,262,527. This is to be paid out of this $45,000,000. They have got the stock, they have got all the money that is paid out of the $244,000,000 less the $21,000,000. Therefore, they have got the
[Mr. Meig-hen.l
stock for nothing. What is the use of discussing in this House whether they paid a dollar for the stock or not ?
I do not know what the $21,000,000 has to do with the stock. That is paid to the Canadian Northern railway on construction.
What did they pay for their stock ?

Suppose we admit for the moment that they paid nothing for the stock, I am going to inquire while I am on my feet who the culprits are. The Canadian Northern Railway Company was an amalgamation of two companies, one of which was an amalgamation of two others. So the Canadian Northern Railway Company was formed, and by the authority of this Parliament the stock was issued to the promoters fully paid.
No.

Unfortunately for the
hon. gentleman I have the statute before me. He thought he could rely on the hon, member foe 'St. John (Mr. Pugsley); I should have thought he would have learned better before now. This is described as chapter 56 of 62-63 Victoria. ' An Act respecting the Canadian Northern railway.' It was enacted that an amalgamation agreement, which is given as a schedule of the statute, between the Winnipeg Great Northern Railway Company-an amalgamation of two original companies-and the Lake Manitoba Railway and Canal Company, should be ratified and that the new company should be known as the Canadian Northern Railway Company. And it was enacted that the following clause of the agreement should be ratified and confirmed by the Parliament of Canada-this being under the Liberal regime of the right hon. gentleman:
6. Each shareholder in the Winnipeg Company shall be entitled to receive and there shall be issued to him by the amalgamated company, one share in the capital stock of the amalgamated company, issued as fully paid up and free from calls and other liability, for every one hundred dollars paid upon the shares held by him in the capital of the Winnipeg Company.
That is an exchange of stock.

That is ratified by the Government supported by the hon. member for St. John. What is this but an exchange of stock?

7. Each shareholder in the Lake Manitoba Company shall be entitled to receive, and there shall be issued to him by the amalgamated company, two shares in the capital stock of the amalgamated company, issued as fully paid up and free from calls and other liability, for every one hundred dollars of fully paid-up stock held by him in the capital of the Lake Manitoba Company.
Under the authority of that statute, Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann got the basic stock of the Canadian Northern railway as fully paid up.
What was the amount?

I do not know, but it "was the whole original stock of the Canadian Northern railway. And every stock authority for which was given by Parliament was given by the Government of the present leader of the Opposition. The original stock, the large amount that was first allotted to these men, was allotted by the Parliament of Canada in 1899 as fully paid up. Now, we shall expect to hear the hon. member for St. John say as we have heard him say so often before, that he was not a member of the House at that time, and that if he had been we should have seen nothing but the blue sky of good government and a complete absence of such enactments as this.

Did not I say this afternoon that the hon. gentleman could not find anywhere a statute declaring the original stock of the company to be fully paid up? That was the statement I made, and the statute which the hon. gentleman reads is entirely in accordance with that statement, because it was simply an exchange of stock by an amalgamated company for shares in the two companies absorbed by the amalgamated company.

This is the original
stock of the Canadian Northern railway. The only difference between this enactment and this is that the hon. gentleman's Government gave two shares for one in the original company, and we are giving one share for two in the original company.

I do not think the Solicitor General has helped his case by his reference to the capital stock of this company. Though he is able to quote statutes as to how the original stock of the Canadian Northern railway was paid up, he did not tell us what the amount of the stock was.
They never paid anything.

So far as the two original companies that merged into the Canadian Northern railway was concerned, we have no information that the stock which they exchanged in the Canadian Northern railway was not fully paid up stock-

But they never paid a
dollar.
The statute the hon gentleman has quoted from does not show that.

That is what hon. gentlemen opposite say-they have been saying that for days and weeks.
Mr. NiEELY: The point is that so far as the original stock is concerned this amount may be so small as to be hardly worth considering. The Solicitor General should have the faets for us. So far as the balance of the present Canadian Northern Railway system is concerned, there is not one bit of evidence that the balance of the stock, apart from the original stock that entered into the Canadian Northern Railway system, ever cost Mackenzie and Mann one single dollar of their own money. The hon. gentleman has not cleared up that point.
The section which we are considering is, I understand, the important part' of the resolution, because it is the section which gives this Government authority to guarantee the bonds of the Canadian Northern to the extent of $45,000,000. It is remarkable that the know-it-all of this agreement, the Solicitor General, is so innocent of the private affairs of Mackenzie and Mann. He does not know, for instance, whether Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, have any interest in the town of Mount Royal at the entrance of the tunnel on the outskirts of the city of Montreal? I wonder if the Solicitor General can tell us anything about the townsite of Port Mann on the Pacific coast, near Vancouver. Does he know whether Mackenzie and Mann have any interest in the townsite of Port Mann, and will he please tell us whether it is included in the Canadian Northern Town Properties Company? Will the hon. Solicitor General answer that, yes or no?
I will inquire while you are on your feet.
Do you know whether it is or not?
I am inquiring now; proceed with your speech.

Then I will stand on my feet until the inquiry is completed. If

the Solicitor General has not that information, he ought to have it.
Carried.

No; I ask the Solicitor General again whether or not the townsite of Port Mann is included in the Canadian Northern Town Properties Company? I have a right to an answer to that question, and I am going to get it.
The hon. gentleman is off his base.
I think the hon. gentleman's request is entitled to some consideration.
The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce does not do credit to his long parliamentary experience by making any such remark as he has just made.
I merely asserted what was a fact: that as the hon. gentleman was standing on his fe'et he was off his base.

Mr. Chairman, I have not had as long a parliamentary experience as my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but if it is my privilege to spend as many years in this Parliament as he has, I hope it will not be recorded against me that I have been off my base as many times as the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce has been. I am waiting for the information for which I have asked.
When the hon. gentleman is through speaking, I purpose answering his question.

I am asking a straight
question, and I should like to have the answer.
Mr.	MEIGHEN:	Town Properties,
Limited, was formed when the last issue of $17,000,000 of land grant bonds was made. That was, I think, in the year 1910. The trust deed, which is on the table of the House, filed by the Government in this connection, gives, if I remember correctly, all the assets that were within the town properties of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited. All those assets go into that trust deed and are now included in this agreement. I am pretty sure the trust deed will tell the hon. gentleman whether or not Port Mann is included; I cannot offhand do so.

Does not my hon. friend the Solicitor General think that he ought to be able before this resolution passes to
CMr. Neely.]
give that information? It certainly does seem to me to be an extraordinary thing that of the two great townsites of the Canadian Northern Railway Company, one at Mount Royal, the eastern terminus at the city of Montreal, has been excluded from the agreement, as my hon. friend himself admits. As to Port Mann, which is the only other great terminal of the Canadian Northern system, my hon. friend is not able to give the committee information as to whether or not it is included.

If the hon. gentleman had understood me rightly, he would have seen that the information is already given and on the table of the House. The amount of data asked for has been so great and the amount given that has not been asked for is so much greater still, that I think the man would be more than human who could remember every little detail of that data.

Port Mann is not a little detail; Port Mann is the great terminal of the Canadian Northern Railway system. Surely my hon. friend, who is promoting this legislation and asking the committee to adopt it, ought to be able to tell us whether or not Port Man:, is included.
I shall be glad to look it up and see.

The Solicitor General
said a few moments ago that in 1899 the Government authorized the issue by the Canadian Northern Railway Company of its capital stock fully paid up and nonassessable. I knew at the time that the hon. gentleman was mistaken. Here is what the statute of 1899 says in reference to the Canadian Northern:
The Winnipeg Company and the Manitoba Company hereby agree to amalgamate and do hereby amalgamate and form one company upon the terms and conditions hereinafter set out. The name of the amalgamated company shall be the Canadian Northern Railway Company.
That was the first time the Canadian Northern Railway Company appeared on the scene.- (Reading):
The amount of the capital stock of the amalgamated company shall be $16,000,000-*
Not $70,000,000; not $92,000,000, but $16,000,000. (Reading):
-divided into 160,000 shares of $100 each. The head office of the amalgamated company shall be at the city of Toronto or at such other place as the board of directors may from time to time by by-law prescribe.
Each shareholder in the Winnipeg Company shall be entitled to receive and there shall be

issued to him by the amalgamated company one share in the capital stock of the amalgamated company, issued as fully paid up and free from calls and liability for every $100 paid up upon the shares held by him in the capital of the Winnipeg Company.
Each shareholder in the Lake Manitoba company shall be entitled to receive, and there shall be issued to him by the amalgamated company, two shares in the capital stock of the amalgamated company, issued as fully paid up and free from calls and other liability, for every $100 of fully paid up stock held by him.
There was no authorization of an issue of stock for nothing. Every share of stock that was fully paid up was handed over, and how can the hon. gentleman stand up here and say that the former Government authorized the issue of $77,000,000 of fully paid-up stock of the Canadian Northern when the capital stock of this company was only $16,000,000. Every dollar's worth of stock had to be paid for, and no stock was issued until it was paid for; so the statement of the Solicitor General is inaccurate, as is all the information that has been received from Mackenzie and Mann in connection with this whole transaction. The Government does not know at this minute whether $45,000,000 is sufficient to complete the road; they have not definite knowledge about the matter. I believe that I have better information myself than the Government has. Hon. gentlemen may smile, but let me say that the Government got its information from Mackenzie and Mann whereas I got mine from men who are absolutely independent of this Parliament, of this Government, and of the Liberal party-railroad men, who know the situation of the Canadian Northern, and who say that instead of $100,000,000 it will take not less than $150,000,000 to complete the road. So this company will have to come back here within two or three years at the outside for $45,000,000 or $50,000,000 more. I just rose to correct the statement of the Solicitor General that the former Government authorized the issue of paid-up capital stock by the Canadian Northern under the Act of 1899.
All I can say is that the hon. gentleman has made a very poor attempt to correct me. I read exactly what was in the Act.
So did I.

The hon. gentleman is now endeavouring to say that because all that was done by the first clause was to grant a fully paid-up share of the Canadian Northern for a fully paid-up share in the Winnipeg company, that therefore the paidup share in the Winnipeg company was paid up in cash. Is that his argument?
I do not know whether it was paid in cash or not.

I did not think he would say it was paid up in cash.
Mr. GERMaN : Mackenzie and Mann put in no cash; they were not the original men in this concern.

They were.
9 p.m. Mr. GERMAN. No, they were not.

Mackenzie and Mann
were the incorporators of the Canadian Northern railway.
Certainly.

And they were the men who were in the Winnipeg and Southeastern railway, and in the Winnipeg and Hudson Bay railway, and in the Lake Manitoba Railway and Canal Company. They brought these three companies together, and a certain amount of stock was issued to them as fully paid up in lieu of their services.
But not authorized by Parliament.

It must have been
authorized by Parliament, or it could not have been issued.
It was not authorized as paid up.

Now I have the point of hon. gentlemen opposite. Though they had this stock in the Lake Manitoba Railway and Canal Company in their possession, it was not issued by 'the authority of Parliament. Then why did the Government give them two shares in the new company for every share they held in the Lake Manitoba Company? Oh, such water! Did you ever hear the Lite? They pour in one hundred per cent of water, and the hon. member for St. John holds the spout.

I think the Solicitor
General would be employed to greater advantage to the people of this country, if he would give this committee the information 'they are entitled to as to whether or not he has made an investigation as to the Canadian Northern Mount Royal townsite, at Montreal, and the Port Mann town-site, the other great townsite of the Canadian Northern on the Pacific coast. My hon. friend has entirely misquoted

me in regard to paid-up stock. I stated this afternoon that there were two ways in which stock might be paid up, one is by a payment of cash; and the other by delivering over property or performing services of value. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance agreed with me in that. There must always be a reasonable consideration for the fully paid-up stock, and in this particular case we all know-the public know because the public are not fools-that Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, have from the outset of this great enterprise, made it a point to secure subsidies and guarantees of bonds for the construction of the different parts of their system. It is true that the stock has been issued and delivered to the contractors, but to say that cash has been paid for this stock is to say what nobody believes to be the case. Legally, it may be paid up in that way.
And rightfully so.

I am not sure about that. I am not sure that it is exactly right for contractors who own all the stock in a company, who own the board of directors, who are building a railway and who receive the proceeds of bonds and cash subsidies for every dollar that the road will cost, I repeat I am not sure that it is the right thing for these stock-holders to get their own board of directors, probably their own employees, to issue that stock to them as fully paid up when it represents no cash paid, and no services rendered. But still it can be done legally, I admit that. I have no doubt that legally this stock is issued as non-assessable stock for services rendered by the contractors. The point I was making this afternoon-and I am sorry my hon. friend seems to delight in misquoting me, although it does not do me any harm, and I do not think it does him any good-was that this Parliament is doing to-day what the courts in Great Britain would declare to be a crime if done by a board of directors; that is, to declare as fully paid up
5100,000,000 of stock which this Parliament knows has not been paid up. At the last session of Parliament the very most that could have been paid up was 570,000,000, as the hon. member for Pictou pointed out this afternoon, somewhat to the discomfiture of, and a source of irritation to, the hon. Minister of Finance, who is generally so calm and genial. The Minister of Finance stated at the last session of Parliament that of that stock the Government was to get one-tenth, or $7,000,000. That was the extent to which any pretense was made that the stock was
[Mr. Pugsley.l
paid up, but to-day Parliament is declaring to the public that the whole $100,000,000, and possibly $125,000,000, is to be regarded as fully paid up and non-assessable, and that is doing what the courts in England would declare to be a crime if done by a board of directors, because there they require that all the stock shall be paid up in cash. And will any gentleman of business experience, no matter how strong may be his Conservative proclivities, say that this $100,000,000 of stock, even as a matter of speculation, is worth more than $5,000,000 or $10,000,000 ? This Parliament is not doing what it ought to do in declaring that this $100,000,000, and possibly $125,000,000, of stock is fully paid up and non-assessable. Surely, as this whole thing is to be carried through by the people of Canada, Parliament ought to shave down the stock instead of increasing it from $77,000,000 to $125,000,000. Parliament ought to cut it down to what any one, in th.e wildest dream of imagination, would say that the equity of redemption was worth namely, from $5,000,000 to $10,000,000 and put it in some ;aafe place as a security for the people of Canada until this railway has been carried through. Why does my hon. friend seek to misrepresent my position? Why does he go back to the statutes of 1899 and vainly try to show that I have made some statements which are not in accordance with the facts? The quotation from the statute does not at all alter the correctness of the statement which I made nor does it alter the correctness of the statement made by my hon. friend from Welland.

The hon. gentleman
said something about my misrepresenting him. I simply stated what he had said and I read the statute against him. He seems to have a great deal of doubt about the moral rectitude of getting stock by anything except by the payment of hard cash and he thinks that we ought to have shaved down this stock to $5,000,000 or $10,000,000. He believes there is no justification in the world", because it was not got by hard cash originally, in leaving it at a greater amount than $5,000,000 or $10,000,000. I have shown that the Government that he supported authorized a capitalization for this company of $16,000,000. Now I have procured out of the Library the statutes of 1901 and I find that in 1901 the Ontario and Rainy River Railway Company was amalgamated also with the Canadian Northern Railway Company and the whole was called the Can-

Adian Northern Railway Company by authority of the late Government. By reference to section 4 of the agreement which was ratified, chapter 52, of the Canadian Northern Railway Act, 1901, the following words aire found:
The amount of the capital stock of the amalgamated company shall be twenty-four million seven hundred and fifty thousand dollars ($24,750, COO) being the total of the capitals of the two companies parties hereto; the said capital shall be divided into shares of one hundred dollars each.
Then, clause 7:
Each shareholder in the Canadian Northern Railway Company shall be entitled to receive and there shall be issued to him by the amalgamated company one share in the capital stock of the amalgamated company issued as fu ly paid up and free from calls and other liability, for every hundred dollars .paid up upon the shares held by him, or to which under any contract with the Canadian Northern Company, he may be or become entitled in the capital of the Canadian Northern Company.
Any contract that Mackenzie, Mann and Company had with the Canadian Northern Railway Company for shares was ratified with the imprimatur of the late Government in that clause.
Clause 8:
Each shareholder in the Rainy River Company shall be entitled to receive and there shall be issued to him by the amalgamated company, one share in the capital stock of the amalgamated company issued as fully paid up and free from calls and other liability for every hundred dollars paid up upon the shares held by him or to which under any contract with the Rainy River Company he may become entitled in the capital stock of the Rainy River Company.
The late Government, in 1901, again raised the capital to $24,750,000 and in so raising it ratified any contract that Mackenzie, Mann and Company had with these two companies to receive stock in lieu of services. Yet my hon. friend has very grave doubts now about the moral rectitude of paying anything for stock except hard cash. Why did not the hon. gentleman shave it down to what the wildest imagination would say it was worth in 1901? The hon. gentleman says there is going to be $125,000,000 of stock in this company, all water, and not worth more than $5,000,000 or $10,000,000. If there is going to be $125,000,000 of this stock, $25,000,000 of it will be paid for in hard cash, our stock amounting to $40,000,000 will be worth par on the market and this country will be $40,000,000 ahead on the deal. Does the hon. gentleman dispute that?
I dispute that the country will be $40,000,000 ahead.

The holders of the $25,000,000 of bonds have to elect to take the stock for their $25,000,000 of bonds before there can be $125,000,000 of stock in this company. Are there any people outside of a lunatic asylum who are going to take $100 stock for a $100 bond unless they are assured that that stock is worth $100? They will have to pay $25,000,000 cash for $25,000,000 of stock and yet the hon. gentleman says that there will be $125,000,000 of stock which will be worth from $5,000,000 to $10,000,000.
We sell $25,000,000 of stock for $25,000,000 cash and pay off $25,000,000 debt with the money. That is what happens when the holders of the convertible bonds surrender their bonds and take stock instead. We will hold, not forty per, cent but 40/125ths, but our 40/125ths is worth as much money after conversion as our forty per cent was worth before. The hon. member says that this stock should not be issued except for hard cash. Will the hon. gentleman be frank enough to admit that a bond guarantee itself is a good consideration for stock in a company? In guaranteeing the bonds of the Canadian Northern and taking $40,000,000 of stock fully paid up is there anything reflecting upon our moral rectitude? Will not that stock be considered, and rightly so, as being fully paid up?
If the hon. gentleman would take my advice I would advise him not to speculate in Canadian Northern stock.

The hon. gentleman
would advise us to get out of office, and let him get in, but the country would not agree with his advice. I am asking him if he believes that a bond guarantee is a good consideration for an issue of stock fully paid up?
I said there were two or three considerations; there might be cash, there might be property, or there might be services rendered.
And a bond guarantee would be a service rendered?
A contract, I think would be.

Then our $40,000,000 is fully paid up, and should be issued to us. This House fully realizes, and the hon. gentleman was good enough to admit, that he was wrong to-night in saying that only

hard cash would do. The reason he had to admit that was that he himself, in 1903, voted the Grand Trunk Railway Company the whole of the common stock. of the Grand Trunk Pacific in consideration of their bond guarantee, and agreed to issue it to them fully paid up. That is why [DOT]he was compelled to admit that a bond guarantee was a very good consideration for fully paid stock.
iMr. PUGSLEY: What I stated was that in this country cash, or the transfer of property, or services rendered, might be a good consideration for paid-up stock. I said that in England they have a different law, and that they will not allow stock to be paid for except by cash.
That it would be a crime to do otherwise.

Does my hon. friend say that in England they are not allowed to issue stock for considerations other than
cash?
I think not now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Then that is very recent, because I know that in England it was perfectly permissible, except that the nature of the property, or other consideration, had to be fully stated and no misrepresentation [DOT]made about it. In hundreds of cases in Great Britain, within the past fifteen or twenty years, I know that has been done. Any man who examines the English reports will know that has been done, and that questions as to misrepresentation in respect to the consideration have been frequently adjudicated upon by the courts. If my hon. friend says that there has been any recent change in the statute, I am not aware of it. The statute must 'be very recent if that is the case.

Does not my right hon. friend know that the way they had of getting around the law in England was to enter the value of the property in the books and make it appear as a cash payment? In the last few years the English Companies Act has been altered, and now all stock must be paid for in cash. I may be wrong; if my right hon. friend expresses douibt about that I would think that he would be in the right, but that is my impression.
