speechtext: I ha/ve not examined the question recently, but I know that was the English Act for long years while I was in active practice.

The Solicitor General has not been able to discover whether the properties of the Townsite Company of Port Mann are to be included in this security of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. It seems to me very strange that this committee is not to get any more definite information with reference to the value of some of these securities that we are taking as a protection against this $45,000,000 bond guarantee to the Canadian Northern Railway Company.

I think I could give the information which the Solicitor General has hesitated to give. I have here a copy of the trust deed made between the Canadian Northern Railway Company, the British Empire Trust Company and the National Trust Company. That is the one, as I understand, that is incorporated in the agreement. By the schedule that appears to be limited entirely to lands in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and would not include the town-site at Port Mann. The fourth schedule speaks of land in the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, in respect of the construction of lines subsidized by the Statutes of Canada, and also of other lands in the said provinces. That will be the three provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. If that is the only schedule bearing on it, then it would appear that not only Port Mann but that all other townsites in British Columbia will be excluded. If I find any others I shall call my hon. friend's attention to it.
Does the hon. gentleman think it is of much value?

I did not think the
occasion was a suitable one for the hon. gentleman to criticise me too severely, because I exercised some care to thank the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) for toeing ready to furnish my hon. friend with the information that I was not able to supply. Before I give information to the House, I endeavour to be certain that I know what I am speaking about, even to the details. The hon. member for St. John ventured the information to the hon. member for Humboldt; and on that information my hon. friend based a very eloquent appeal. He has asserted to the House that this Port Mann townsite is a very valuable site, as valuable as all the rest that we did include; that it .should have been included, and particularly that these new townsites in British Columbia, as a matter of gross carelessness, were not included. I think I shall be able to show the hon. gentleman that I am the person he ought to thank and not the hon. member for St. John. The hon. member for St.

John has misinformed him. The townsite of Port Mann is included.

I object to the Solicitor
General putting into my mouth words that I did not use. I did not say that the town-site of Port Mann was a valuable piece of property. I said that it was probably on a par with other townsites along the Canadian Northern.

I thought the value
would go down right away. I expected a drop in the value.
'Hansard' will show what I said.

I was saying that the hon. member for St. John had misinformed my hon. friend from Humboldt. This document has been on the table for days. It has been the property of every hon. member. It is a long document; but I find in the third schedule that the townsite of Port Mann is included.
Is that in the trust deed?

There are several here anyway. I do not know just how many -in the document which the hon. gentleman is reading, at page 43-the third schedule, part 1. A reference to page 7 will show that it is included in the mortgage :	i
All the right, title, estate and interest of the company in the properties and premises mentioned in the said, third schedule, but subject as to such of the properties and premises as have been sold or agreed to be sold to the agreements entered into for the sale or disposition thereof.
What is my hon. friend reading from?

I am reading from the trust deed of the 19th of November, 1913.
The hon. gentleman from Humboldt says that the townsite of Port Mann and others have been milked, all but these new ones in British Columbia. I am in a position to inform the hon. gentleman, that the proceeds of the townsites, that came in before Canadian Northern Town Properties, Limited, was formed, were reinvested in further townsites; and as a result, those proceeds form part of the assets of Town Properties, Limited, and come in under this mortgage.
In what further townsites were they invested?

They are all named in this document. There are a number of pages of townsites alone. Pages 38, 39, 40,

41, 42, 43, 44, 45 and half of page 46 are all names of townsites included in the assets of Towns Properties, Limited.
The hon. gentleman repeated also an alleged argument that I heard very recklessly advanced the other day, namely, that, because they had been made subject to the 4 per cent perpetual bond mortgage of 1903, consequently there could not be any equity in them; there could not be any benefit in taking a subsequent mortgage.

Will my hon. friend
state under what clause in the resolution Port Mann is included?
Under sub-clause (d) of clause 1. It is a part of Town Properties, Limited.

But the Canadian Northern Town Properties, Limited, includes only the equity of redemption of Mackenzie and Mann in the $10,000,000 of capita! stock and the $10,000,000 of debenture stock mentioned in the trust deed.

Certainly, and those
$10,000,000 of capital stock and the $10,000,000 of debenture stock represent all the assets of Town Properties, Limited. What else could represent them?

My hon. friend is mistaken in that. Those $10,000,000 of stock and $10,000,000 of debenture stock are owned by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited; and it is only on that stock, the common stock and the debenture stock, that a charge is created by this agreement. That stock is subject to an outstanding mortgage to the British Empire Trust Company for $17,500,000. It does not take in Port Mann at all.
I do not know how to explain so obvious a fallacy.
Let me read this.
Yes, that will be better.
The eighth clause? [DOT]

No, the reference to it. My hon. friend will see that in the agreement between the Government and the company its reference is to the subsidiary companies mentioned in the eighth clause of the trust deed. That does not show what company that is. I should have grave doubts of the statement of my hon. friend that it includes Port Mann.

The hon. gentleman
surely sees that Port Mann is in the same position as the other townsites.

No, it is not. Clause
9 of the trust mortgage mentions specifically mortgaged lands in the fourth schedule. It would require a Philadelphia lawyer to tell what it means.

We will trust the hon. member for St. John to learn what it means. I am a little in doubt whether the hon. member is trying to create the impression that he was not in error before or whether he does not understand this agreement.
I do not think the hon. gentleman himself understands it.

I understand it most
thoroughly. Naturally, in the trust deed [DOT]there would be different clauses speaking of different classes of property. Some property is owned by Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited; some is not owned entirely by them, because, as the hon. gentleman surely knows, frequently the townsite company will procure from the owner of the land a conveyance of the land under agreement to give back to the owner every other lot or the agreement that shall issue covering every other lot. There is another class of property that has already been sold. So, there are different schedules. But all are added together and become the assets of Town Properties, Limited, and then stock and bonds are issued to Mackenzie and Mann. One schedule refers to these assets that belongs to Mackenzie and Mann. Another schedule speaks of Mackenzie and Mann's interest. Now, the stock and bonds are pledged to secure the $17,500,000 perpetual bond issue, along with the stock and bonds of other companies and along with the assets of the Canadian Northern railway as well. There is, in addition, the equity in the land grant and on the basis of the sales of the lands themselves -because nearly all the land is sold-there is more than enough money coming out of the land to pay the whole land grant bond issue, and the equity is fixed in that laud grant bond mortgage at between $11,000,000 and $12,000,000 as I told the House when I spoke of these resolutions. The hon. gentleman charged me because, as he said, we had made no estimate of the equity in this property. We made an estimate, and that estimate has been given to the House but the hon. gentleman has forgotten it. He is asking, as others have asked, very carelessly, if there is any equity here seeing that the mortgage is perpetual. As I am on my feet, let me answer that. The fact that there is a perpetual mortgage against the property does not argue that there is no equity against the property. Suppose that you, Mr. Chairman, .are the owner of a farm valued at $10,000 against which there is .a perpetual mortgage of $2,000. You still have an equity of $8,000. It is true you are not allowed to pay off the mortgage and must pay interest, say, $100 a year. But who would say that there was no value in the second mortgage on that property? The second mortgagee becomes entitled to all

the rents and profits ever and above the annual charge of over $100. In the same way, we become entitled to all the rents and profits over and above the land grant bond issue on all the properties that went in to secure the perpetual bond mortgage. The fact that the mortgage is perpetual does not affect the value of the equity of redemption.
I desire to get some information with regard to properties in the county of Inverness belonging to the Inverness railway and Coal Company. Is that included?
No.

Why is this very valuable property not included? I may enumerate the properties there. There is sixty miles of well equipped railway extending from the strait of Can so to Mackenzie and Mann's coal property in Inverness. There is a coal mine there which has been operated for eight or nine years with very substantial output. It is estimated that this coal property contains about 40,000,000 tons of coal. This coal company also owns another coal property further north, and also a very large amount of real estate in. the town of Inverness, assessed, I think, in the vicinity of $200,000-a low estimate, of course. I am anxious to see this asset included for two reasons. The first, a selfish one, perhaps is that if this railway were included in the schedule it would come under authority of the Railway Commission. This is important for the people of Inverness, for we have many grievances there with respect to freight, etc. If we had these properties ini-eluded in the schedule we would have an opportunity to appeal to the board that would have the power to give us relief. Another matter of even greater importance is that this road is really an unfinished road. I expected to find it enumerated in the list on page 10 of the documents. The Inverness and Richmond Railway Company sold their charter to Mackenzie and Mann or to what is known as the Inverness Railway and Coal 'Company. This company undertook to construct a road from the strait of Canso to Cheticamp. They built as far as Inverness, that is as far as their own property. Besides getting a double subsidy of $6,400 a mile from the Dominion, they got a subsidy of $4,000 a mile from the local Government and also got a bonus of

$1,000 a mile and free right of way from the municipality of Inverness. Here is the important point.
In chapter 107 of the Nova Scotia statutes of 1898 will be found the agreement which was signed by Mackenzie and Mann for the Inverness Railway and Coal Company, under which they agreed after getting the free right of way and the bonus oi $1,000 a mile for the completion of the road to Inverness, to complete the road to Cheticamp, provided that the Dominion and local subsidies were available. The Dominion and local subsidies have been available every year since the road to Inverness was finished. I ask the Government to insist that Mackenzie and Mann carry out that agreement with the municipality of Inverness. If they refuse to do so, I say that the least they should do is to refund the moneys they have received by way of bonus and free right of way to the town of Inverness. It is certain that the taxpayers of Inverness would never have agreed to pay these men a dollar if they had understood that the road was not to he completed to Cheticamp. I am afraid that the free right of way and the bonus of $1,000 a mile were obtained from the taxpayers of Inverness under false pretenses, because from the very day that Mackenzie and Mann got the money they never made any attempt to show the people of Inverness that their promise to complete the road as far as Cheticamp was made in good faith. This is a very important matter to the people of North Inverness, and I should like to know what is the view of the Government in the matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The particular enterprise to which my hon. friend refers is more largely, as I understand it, a coal mining enterprise than a railway enterprise. It is probable that any considerable amount of capital required to be invested in the enterprise in the early future, except in respect of the extension to which the hon. gentleman alludes, would be an investment of capital in the coal mining part of the proposition and that hardly seems to be within the purview of what Parliament is proposing to do at this moment. Moreover, it is a part of the company's property that is somewhat distant from their main lines. The same is true, to some extent, of the Halifax and Southwestern railway, although that does connect more directly with the Intercolonial and in that way is more directly connected with the main lines than the one to which my hon. friend refers. I am not aware of the difficulty which has

arisen between the company and the municipality of Inverness. I have sent for the statute, however; I will look over it and give my best consideration to what my hon. friend has said.	[DOT]

I wish to ask the right bon. Prime Minister if when these resolutions were under consideration between the Government and the agents of the Canadian Northern railway, the question of terminals for Sydney harbour and of making Sydney harbour a port of call for the Canadian Northern Atlantic liners was under consideration?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I cannot say that it was specially under consideration.

I hold in my hand a
telegram which I feel in duty bound to! place before the Government and on * Hansard as it was sent to mer by the secretary of the Board of Trade of Sydney. It is dated April 7, and is as follows:
The following resolution was passed by the Sydney Board of Trade to-day, and it is desired that a resolution along this line be introduced in the provincial legislature.
Whereas Sydney is looking for deep-water terminals, which, it is hoped, will be shortly installed here, and whereas the Canadian Northern Railway Company is now asking the Dominion Government to guarantee a new bond issue, and whereas the Government is now considering this request; therefore resolved that the Government be memorialized that before the granting of this assistance the Canadian Northern Railway Company be required to guarantee that as soon as adequate docking facilities are provided at Sydney their incoming and outgoing boats make this a port of call, cutting out the Belle Isle route entirely during the open season; and further resolved that a copy of this resolution be sent to the right hon. Premier Borden, to the Premier of Nova Scotia and to the representatives of this county at Ottawa and at Halifax.
Ross O. Evans,
Secretary. I
I do not know what gave rise to the report which I have heard that the matter was discussed between the Canadian Northern authorities and the Government. I had a letter from a gentleman-and I desire to say that he is in no way connected, so far as I know, with the Canadian Northern railway, with Mackenzie and Mann, or with the firm of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited-suggesting to me that it would be in my interests not to oppose this legislation, in view of the fact that the city of Sydney would be very materially assisted by the establishment of dry-docks or of shipping and harbour facilities there which would accommodate the ocean liners
of Mackenzie and Mann. I may say that I did not pay very much attention to that document; what I want to find out from the Government is whether the matter was discussed-it has apparently been brought to the attention of the Prime Minister- and whether it is the intention of the Government to afford facilities in the harbour of Sydney by way of accommodating the liners of Mackenzie and Mann. So far as I am personally concerned, anything that would make for the betterment of Sydney harbour or for the constituency which I have the honour to represent would receive my very hearty support, but at the same time I do not think' I would go so far as to say that because Sydney harbour would be somewhat benefited by this legislation, I .would be in honour bound to vote for resolutions which would not otherwise, perhaps, receive my support.
The resolutions before you, Mr. Chairman, are very important. I do not pretend to have given the matter very serious consideration; I have left that to minds that are more able to grasp such matters than mine. But a few things have been bothering me considerably in connection with these resolutions. Mackenzie and Mann have asked this Government to guarantee a bond issue of $45,000,000. That in itself, in connection with a transcontinental line, would not be such a very serious matter, but when we consider that this concern has received many millions-and hundreds of millions-of dollars in the shape of properties and money from the people of Canada and that they are now asking for the guarantee of an additional $45,000,000 of stock, it does become a serious matter. I am not going to charge the Government with not having given this matter the very serious consideration which it requires.
I believe that an investigation should be held into Mackenzie and Mann's dealings in railway matters right from the start of their career as railway promoters. One thing that struck me as being very peculiar was that a gentleman should send an affidavit to this Government swearing that to the best of his knowledge Messrs. Mackenzie and Mann never received a dollar by way of profits or otherwise from the Canadian Northern railway. Why should not Mackenzie and Mann do the manly thing and swear to this affidavit themselves? Surely they have more knowledge of what benefits have accrued to them through their railway promotions in this country than has any clerk or private secretary connected with the firm. I would like to see an investiga-

tion held to find out exactly what Mackenzie and Mann have taken out of their railway enterprises in this country. I am not in a position to state that they have made a single dollar, but I think they are not dealing with the Government in the proper way when they get a clerk-perhaps I should not say a clerk, because he may be a very important official in that company-to make an affidavit which would have come with far better grace from themselves. That was one of the things that first raised a suspicion in my mind that their dealings with the Government were not altogether above board. I am not one of those who believe that the Canadian Northern transcontinental should be refused assistance where assistance is necessary and be allowed to die, so to speak. I believe that this undertaking, having had the approval of the people of Canada in the impress of a statute, so to speak, should not be allowed to go down. While the people of this country should not throw that road aside, I do not think there would be that crisis which has been predicted if the bonds were not guaranteed to the full extent of the $45,000,000. I read the other day an article from the Financial Post of Montreal which is, I presume, well acquainted with financial matters in this country, or at least it pretends to be. While they approve of the Government of Canada coming to the assistance of Mackenzie and Mann, they admit in an editorial that if assistance were not given to the full extent proposed, nothing like a great financial crisis would arise in this country. Instead of the Government introducing this legislation in the dying days of the session, would it not be better to come to the assistance of the Canadian Northern railway and Mackenzie and Mann by helping them to keep their heads above water until a full investigation has been held ? I would like to see the contractors and the workmen who have built roads for Mackenzie and Mann get paid as quickly as possible, but I take the ground that the most this Government should do at this session of Parliament is to give the Canadian Northern railway and Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, just a sufficient amount to keep them floating until they have been examined under oath as to their dealings in railway matters in this country since 1896. That is what commends itself to me, but I am only speaking for myself.
In regard to the matter which I have
TMr. Carroll ]
brought to the attention of the right hon. Premier, I may say that the feeling in the eastern section of the province of Nova Scotia has been accentuated by the impression that the Canadian Northern Railway Company may get running rights over the Intercolonial. I am not one of those who think that the granting to a transcontinental railway of running .rights over the government system of railways is naturally a bad thing, because it may develop into a very good thing. I can only say that if the time comes when Mackenzie and Mann will have running rights over the Intercolonial and railway facilities in the city of Sydney, any legislation introduced by this Government to provide adequate docking facilities in that harbour will have my own personal support. I could not do otherwise, representing, as I do, the city of Sydney.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I know that some persons who have a very great interest in the development of the harbour at Sydney did bring this subject during the last few weeks to the attention of Mackenzie, Mann and Company, Limited, and the Canadian Northern railway. I think Sir William Mackenzie himself was seen on the subject. I was also spoken to by the same gentlemen, but as a great many matters had to be dealt with in connection with the subject now under discussion, we did not feel that there was time or opportunity to take up that other matter just at this time. Furthermore, my hon. friend will realize that it will be practically impossible to make an arrangement of that kind with only one line of steamships engaged in carrying the mails. I do not think it would be wise to deal with the subject in that piecemeal way. For these reasons we have not been able to give the subject that consideration which it undoubtedly deserves.

If at any time the Government considers this proposal, I would commend to the Prime Minister and the members of the Government certain reports that were made some years ago concerning Sydney harbour as .a port of call for mails. A test was made in 1906 of carrying the mails from Sydney to Montreal, and if I remember rightly it was shown that the mails would reach Montreal much more quickly when taken off at Sydney than if taken off at St. John or Halifax. I think the report will be very useful when this, subject comes up for consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I remember the occasion fo which my hon. friend alludes.

speechtext: Of the persons ?
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think a detailed statement has been given of them. I am quite sure that we have one, but I did not think it was desirable to place it on the table of the House. If my hon. friend desires to look at it, I shall not have the slightest objection.
Not at the moment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Subject to correction, I
think the Solicitor General, who has been called away to Toronto to-night, showed me a list of the various persons'to whom these moneys are owing.

That was the feature ot
the case that I wanted to draw attention to. Until I have seen the statement I do not know how far my argument will be borne out by it, but I want to draw attention to the fact that the list of enterprises which are to be benefited by the expenditure of the money to be provided does not include the Canadian Northern Western, or the Canadian Northern Saskatchewan companies. The Saskatchewan company is chartered by the provincial Government, it is not under Dominion charter, but I do
not know whether the Alberta company is under Dominion charter or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The Canadian Northern Alberta is under Dominion charter.

The Canadian Northern

It is a provincial company.

I was not sure whether

Their bonds are guaranteed by the provincial governments for the purpose of securing the construction of certain lines. They do not appear in the list of companies upon whose lines any portion of this expenditure is to be made At the same time I notice in the resolution that they are brought under Dominion jurisdiction by being declared to be railways for the general advantage of Canada, and I notice further that in the covenant between the company and the Government the stock of both these companies is transferred to the Canadian Northern Railway Company.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What page is that?

On page 15 which gives
a schedule of the companies whose stock is transferred to the Canadian Northern and in which these two companies appear. These companies are left entirely dependent upon the provincial Government for their construction, but they are taken under the authority, control and jurisdiction of the Dominion Government and their stock is made a part of the property of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. That is all made subject to the blanket mortgage that the Government propose to take.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The stock would be but
not the physical assets. The physical assets of any of these roads will only become subject to the mortgage in case of any portion of the moneys provided by these guaranteed securities is expended either in construction, or completion, or betterment, and to the extent to which the moneys are so expended. As far as the stock is concerned, that is different, of course.

These two companies are left to their own resources, they are left to the provincial governments tor their com-

plete construction and in so far as they are dealt with under this arrangement, it is an impediment, if not an actual bar, to the raising of further moneys on the open market for the purpose of completing these enterprises.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In -what way?

I shall be very glad to show that. So far as they are brought under the terms of this general mortgage-if very little, then the effect will be very little; if largely the effect will be large-the effect of the blanket mortgage will be- to act as either an impediment or as an actual bar to the raising of further money upon the securities of these lines.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If there is any detriment to any of these companies we shall be glad indeed to make any modifications to meet the views of my hon. friend. There is no desire to hinder or impede these companies in raising the money necessary to complete their road. If any portion of the money raised by the guaranteed securities should be applied in assisting the construction of the roads to which the hon. member alluded, or in providing betterments, then, of course, under the terms of the guarantee, the physical assets of the roadi will be made subject to the mortgage ito that extent. But if, on the other hand, as he suggests, no portion of these moneys is proposed to be expended upon those roads, then nothing would stand in the way of making a further charge on the physical assets because the physical assets in that case wouldi not become subject in any way to the provision of this mortgage. The control of the company by means of the disposition of its stock is a different thing; that would be transferred to the Canadian Northern railway. But, as my hon. friend knows, that would not result in an actual change in the management of the road, because it would continue to be managed by the same interests as before. That is the way I look at the situation, and if my hon. friend has a criticism upon that or any further suggestions to offer I can assure him I shall be very glad to consider them.
At the moment I am only looking for information, and I am not able to arrive altogether at what I want unless I see the actual proposition of the Government before the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am anxious to get my hon. friend's point of view.

My hon. friend says that these roads will not be prejudiced in the raising of further money on the security of their physical assets unless money is expended upon them, when a security will be taken. If there is an expenditure upon the roads for the purpose of securing furtherance of betterment or completion, a mortgage is taken for that. That, of course, will certainly have the effect of prejudicing any attempt that may be made to raise further money to carry these roads further on. The mortgage that has been taken, let it be large or small, will be a detriment to the subsequent mortgage that will require to be taken. On the other hand, if there is no expenditure there will be no mortgage, there will be no impediment so far as that is concerned; but there will be this condition, that the road has been made subject not only to the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners but, in case of default, to the jurisdiction of the Government, and to that extent there is a possibility of prejudice against the success of the attempt to raise further moneys in order to push the road farther forward.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Would my hon. friend suggest to me why making the road subject to the Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada would prejudice any attempt to raise further money?

That is not what creates the prejudice. The prejudice is not in the condition that the road continues to exist and to be operated, but the prejudice is that in case of default a change of conditions and authority takes place, and there is no assurance that after that default takes place that particular branch, and it would be a branch of the system, would be operated a3 a part of the system. As the Solicitor General said the other night, the very reason an amalgamation has not taken place is so that in case of default, or even, I think he said, without default, it would be possible for the Government, by foregoing their security on any section, to discharge themselves from obligation and leave it on its own resources. Everybody knows that you cannot operate a single short line of railway at a profit. The experience of the Maritime provinces in connection with the Intercolonial railway shows that. The provinces have guaranteed these lines for the purpose of their being operated in connection with a general system. Unless they are to be operated in connection with that general system, there is going to be an unexpected burden upon the provincial

guarantors. If the Government is coming before Parliament to say: We will take the responsibility of seeing that these branch lines are carried to completion, that they are brought to a proper stage of construction for successful operation, there is no difficulty in the matter. But if the Government say, as they do say: We are not going to take any part of this money to extend or improve these particular branch lines, and they are to be left to the provinces to be done with as they may be able to do with them, my theory is that the position of the provinces is going to be seriously prejudiced; and my desire in asking to know where the expenditure is to be made is to-find out how far the Government propose to go in carrying out necessary extensions and betterments of the system as it stands at present. There is much in support of the suggestion that once the blanket mortgage is put on the system it will not be possible-certainly it will not be possible for the Canadian Northern railway-to go on the money market and raise additional moneys for the further extension or betterment of their property. I think that will be conceded, that once the further mortgage has been placed upon the properties, these properties will be shut out of the money markets of the world. That being the case, it is absolutely important that there should be a thorough understanding before that mortgage is put on, before this agreement is ratified, as to just exactly how far	it is intended to carry
the work of railway extension and development in these two prairie provinces. To my mind that is the most important and most serious feature of the arrangement. Not to delay the House, but just to repeat the condition that exists in the constituency that I represent, I may say that we have a large settlement in the Peace River country on Grande Prairie. Eight or ten townships there are under occupation. People have gone in there during the last two or three years, and they are going in there now. That settlement is 300 miles from Edmonton; the country is very difficult to traverse, and the settlement there can be reached only under very great difficulties. The Canadian Northern have a charter from Edmonton to Grande Prairie. They have a guarantee from the provincial Government for a hundred miles of the line. Some forty miles of line have been ironed, and the balance of the hundred miles has been partly graded. That leaves 200 miles of intervening territory where no grant has 258
been given by the province or by the Dominion and where no work has been done. I am anxious first of all to know whether that hundred miles is going to be completed, and then I am anxious to know what is going to happen in regard to the remaining 200 miles necessary to reach the settlement now in occupation of that territory. It is a matter that is vital to the development of western Canada. We have alienated the greater part of the pTairie of the West. The Peace River is the country of the future, the country to which people are going, and it is to the settlement of that country that we must look for the future . increase in the development of the western country. If this aid means that that road, for instance, is to be carried to completion, then to that, extent good work is being done; but if it means that the further carrying forward of that enterprise is to be stopped, that is a very serious question, and certainly I would think that the country, instead of being benefited, would be prejudiced to a very great degree.
What exists in a northwesterly direction from Edmonton exists in almost similar degree northeast of it. There are settlements there for a distance of one hundred and fifty miles along and north of the Saskatchewan river, from sixty, eighty to one hundred imiles from a railway. The Canadian Northern line is chartered to run through that country. The provincial government has guaranteed bonds for one hundred miles, of which some fifteen or twenty miles have been graded, but nothing has been done to the balance. We want to know if, under this aid, those one hundred miles are to be completed, and what is1 to happen to the people living beyond the end of the one hundred miles. It is veTy desirable, no doubt, to carry the Canadian Northern enterprise forward; but unless, in carrying that enterprise forward, we are going to protect the development of the country, which, after all, is the soul and heart of the Canadian Northern, we are certainly not meeting the requirements of the case. What alarms me is that the arguments that have been put before the House and the country have all pointed to the purpose of this aid as being to relieve the financial situation of the Canadian Northern Railway Company by providing for the completion of its main line. For the past two years we have seen money being poured out by the Canadian Northern Railway Company in building in British Columbia, in building between Port Arthur and Ottawa, while the lines in the prairie west have been



standing still, where the development of the country has been retarded, where people have been disappointed because of the failure to construct, as it was expected would be done. It is a great thing to have a third transcontinental line; it is a great thing to do something to avert unfortunate financial conditions; but if we are going to use money to build railroads where there are no people and to leave the country where the people are without railroads, and generally to tie up the situation so that they are not going to get railroads in the near future, we are going to do the Dominion of Canada a great deal more harm than good. This is a very large amount of money to be raised on the credit of the people of the Dominion, and I assume that we cannot keep <jn doing this every year. If we tie ourselves up this year for a guarantee of $45,000,000, we shall not be in a position next year to meet the requirements if they are not met under the present arrangement. I think it is most important that the application of this arrangement to the railway development of the two western provinces should have more full consideration in the arrangement and in the discussion than it has yet received.
Just in line with what I have said, I read in the Ottawa Journal this evening an editorial. The Evening Journal is a paper very strongly supporting the Government and very strongly supporting this arrangement, and, it is to be presumed, in the confidence of the Government so far as its policy is concerned. The editorial is headed, ' No Confiscation Policy.' I do not want to read the whole editorial, but the last paragraph is as follows:
Mackenzie and Mann have secured from provincial governments of Canada considerable cash and land and a vast amount of bond guarantees. The provinces are getting value in railway expenditures and railway operation. The fact that they did not in other respects look out for their own security does not call on the Borden Government to exterminate Mackenzie and Mann and steal what the provinces gave them. I
I do not know how far the writer of that article understood the situation. I do not know how far he is in the confidence of the Government or how far he expresses the Government ideas; but the connection of the Canadian Northern Railway system with the two western provinces which have largely become financially responsible for the undertaking is not a matter of secondary interest. It is a matter of primary interest to the welfare of this country, and should certainly have, not second, but first con- [DOT]

slderation at the hands of the Government in dealing with this railroad problem.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I entirely agree with my hon. friend in his appreciation of the importance of the matter to which he has alluded. I do not know whether I can make the situation clear to him as it appears to me; but in the first place let me say that there is not any blanket mortgage on the whole Canadian Northern system proposed by these resolutions. There is a mortgage proposed upon the physical assets of the Canadian Northern railway, with the further proviso that, if any of these moneys should be paid out by the Canadian Northern railway to any of the allied companies, then a mortgage upon the physical assets of that particular company shall be taken for the amount so paid out and expended in constructing or completing such railway or in betterments upon it. Therefore, as I said before, I do not think that the raising of money upon the physical assets of any of the branch line railways is in any way prejudiced by the resolutions now proposed.
I am perfectly aware that the provincial Governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan have given a guarantee of bonds in respect of several branch lines of the Canadian Northern railway under different charters and under different names. Now, my hon. friend points out that in respect to certain of these lines in the province of Alberta, it is not, apparently, intended by the Canadian Northern railway that any portion of the sums raised shall be expended on these lines. That is the point.
To start with.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: As I understand the matter the construction of these particular lines, so far as arrangements have been made, is provided for by the securities guaranteed by the provincial government. And if I am not mistaken it is rather desired by one of the provincial Governments at least that the construction shall be left in that way. The question arises then as to a declaration that these particular lines are works for the general advantage of Canada, and there is possibly some force in the suggestion that until these roads are completed at least, they should remain under the control of the provincial Governments. I do not know whether my hon. friend was alluding to that feature.
That is included, although that is not the main thing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, the point is as to whether or not any portion of this money is to be used to extend these lines. As far as that feature is concerned, we were asked to give certain assistance for the purpose of completing the Canadian Northern system. We understood that so far as these provincial lines are concerned, adequate provision would be made under the provincial guarantees. At all events, we asked the company to give us a statement of what requirements were necessary ' for the completion of the system as submitted to us. That statement, as made to us, involved the provision of about $42,000,000 more than seemed to be available at the present time, and so we have brought down these resolutions. What effect will that have upon the development of the branch lines in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan? At least it will have this effect, that if the Canadian Northern Railway system as a system were allowed to collapse and no aid at all were forthcoming at the present juncture, the construction of any lines which have been undertaken as branch lines of that system would, it seems to me, be very greatly delayed. Therefore, so far as that is concerned, we believe that by coming to the aid of the system at the present time and by the endeavour, which we believe will be successful, to place the whole system on a sound financial basis, we shall give a very practical assurance of the extension at an earlier day than otherwise would be possible of the lines to which the hon. gentleman alludes. I am not aware that any application has been made to us for aid out of this sum now proposed to be raised to extend thet particular lines to which he alludes, because, as I understood, the provincial Governments were prepared to implement their guarantees to a further extent for the development of these branch lines. The main line, I think, has been regarded by both the late Administration and the present Administration as a read which should be assisted with federal aid, with the exception of the line through the province of British Columbia, which was initiated by arrangement made with the Government of the province of British Columbia. So far as that was concerned, recognizing, as we did that the system had acquired the status of a transcontinental line and as the development of branch lines throughout the territories would probably he expedited and assisted by putting the main line on the 2581
basis of a transcontinental system, we did assist the line in the province of British Columbia. I do not know whether I have covered all the points which the hon. gentleman brought to my attention, but if there is anything further he wishes me to refer to, I shall be glad to do so.

The other point that I would like the Prime Minister to elaborate a little more is as to the possible effect of the measurable amalgamation that has taken place upon the raising money upon these provincial lines after a general mortgage has been placed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know whether I can add very much of value to what I have already said on that point. Let us take one of these lines-my hon. friend mentioned several. Will he recall the name of one?

The Canadian Northern
Western.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Let us take the Canadian Northern Western line. It has been partially built and remains to be completed for a certain distance, I think my hon. friend said about a hundred miles, through the moneys derived from securities guaranteed by the provincial government. Let us assume that the proceeds of the securities so guaranteed would be sufficient for the completion of these one hundred miles of railway. Let us suppose further that no portion of the aid now proposed is devoted to the completion or any betterments. The physical assets of that line, then, would remain free from this mortgage and would not be affected by it. But as it is included in the list ot roads whose stock is to be transferred to the Canadian Northern railway, then the stock, instead of being vested in Mackenzie and Mann, will .be vested in the Canadian Northern railway and will be subject to the mortgage. That really means that the Canadian Northern railway would own the stock and would control, in the future as in the past, the management and operation of the road. But in case of default and of the vesting of the mortgaged premises either in the Government or in some corporation appointed for the purpose, the management would be changed. I think it will be apparent to my hon. friend-it is apparent to me-that if such a thing were brought about the road would still continue to be part of the great transcontinental system, that is a branch line directly connected with the transcontinental system, a feeder of that system, and, so far as one can foresee, the position of the people of the

province of Alberta whose interests are more *directly concerned in this road would not be in any way prejudiced; because if default were brought about and it were necessary to reorganize the system or if it should pass to the people of Canada for operation as a state-owned railway, or for *operation under lease granted by the Government of Canada to some corporation constituted for the purpose, the branch railway would at least maintain as advantageous a status as that which it has to-day. If my hon. friend has any suggestions to make, I shall be only too glad to receive them.

Unfortunately I am not a *corporation lawyer, and I am rather at a loss in attempting to argue this question. My theory is that, in the first place, the fact that the stock is not available for the purposes of the company will prejudice the financial position of the company in the case of more money being desired to be raised. In the second place, the possibility of change of ownership in case of default would prejudice the possibility of raising money upon the security of the road. If in this legislation the Government specifically provided that in case of default and the taking over of the road by the Government, they would assume the responsibility of the obligations in that regard, then the position would be good. But so long as that question is left in uncertainty, we are legislating here in the face of a possible change of ownership without providing any guarantee as to what shall take place when that change of ownership occurs. My theory, therefoire, is that there is to that extent a prejudice against the road being able to raise further money that may be required in order to carry it forward to completion. My suggestion is that this condition could be remedied by the legislation specifically providing what shall be done if default should occur.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not think that these roads are in any different position from any other portion of the system in that respect. The railway is the modern highway of the world; persons who undertake to build a railway have a certain obligation to operate it, and it would be appropriate to enforce that operation through effective means, by legislation or otherwise, if the persons entrusted with the duty of operating the line did not operate it. If such an obligation rests upon a corporation organized for the purpose of operating a railway, I am sure that my hon. friend will realize that it rests in still greater fMr. Borden.]
measure upon a government, whether of the Dominion or of a province, which by reason of its guarantee and foreclosure of the mortgage securing the bonds so guaranteed, has to take over a road. My hon. friend says that possible change of ownership may prejudice this road. Well, there would be a possibility of change of ownership under the bonds guaranteed by the provincial government, and there would be a possibility of change of ownership of the same character with respect to every road that is enumerated in the list set out in the resolution.

The provincial government is furnishing the money to build these roads, but the ownership of the roads is going to rest in the Canadian Northern Railway Company, or ultimately in the Dominion Government. That is not as good for the province which has provided the money to build the road as if the ownership rested in the Canadian Northern with a reversion to the provincial government. The provincial government, if it had a reversionary interest in the ownership of the road, might he in a position to dispose of the property to some other system, but it is debarred from doing this under these resolutions, where the ownership of the stock, and, therefore, the ultimate ownership of the road, rests in the Canadian Northern, or, in case of default, in the Dominion Government. I submit that the interests of the province are prejudiced to that extent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I can hardly agree with my hon. friend that they are prejudiced to any extent whatever by the fact that the road might ultimately come into the ownership of the people of Canada and become part of a great transcontinental system. I cannot see, with all deference to my hon. friend, that that would prejudice the interests of Alberta. So far as stock is concerned, the road itself is still in the same ownership as before. The only difference is that formerly Mackenzie and Mann, Limited, owned the stock, and now the Canadian Northern railway own the stock. The road is there as an entity, and the corporation which owns it is there as an entity, the same as before. The mere fact that the stock will pass out of the ownership of Mackenzie and Mann into the ownership of the Canadian Northern railway cannot, according to my humble comprehension, and with all due deference to my hon. friend, in the slightest degree

40S3
affect the possibility of raising money for the extension or betterment of the road. I cannot see that there is any possible reason why there should be any such prejudice as my hon. friend suggests.

The province pays, and the Dominion owns and controls; that cannot be as sound a position for the province as if the province, doing the paying, also controlled, and, under certain circumstances, might own. It looks to me like a ease in which the province is, in the slang of the day, left holding the bag, while the Canadian Northern and the Dominion obtain whatever benefit there is from the transaction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I think that if the position of the road is affected at all, it is affected for the better, because it can only be taken over by the Government in case of default in the way that I have mentioned, as part of a great transcontinental system. Why that should be regarded as prejudicing it. I cannot understand. Of course, the Government taking it over in that way would have to assume all obligations in connection with it.
That is the suggestion I made, but it is not made a part of the resolution.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: But it is the practical effect of it, because the Government can only take it over subject to existing obligations, and that is specifically provided in the resolutions. The only persons who are being eliminated in the cases suggested are Mackenzie and Mann. The province is not being eliminated; the province can not be eliminated, because its rights are secured by an outstanding mortgage which protects it. If the Government of Canada ever takes over that road or any of these roads, it must take them over subject to all the existing outstanding obligations upon them.

I quite understand that,
but the Dominion Government does not need to take them over unless it wants to. The Solicitor General in his explanation the other night said that we could cut off any branch lines that we did not wish to take over. That would leave the provinces at a loss with what under other circumstances would be a profitable enterprise. When the Dominion Government is taking the responsibility of putting these roads under the Dominion Railway Act, and is taking the control and ownership of the stock, the circumstances call for the Government s putting in actual legislation what the right hon. gentleman has said would follow in the natural course of events; that is, that the Dominion Government in case of default will take over the branch lines and become responsible for them. If they put that on the face of the document the road is in a position to go to the money markets, and to get further money if it is required, but without that assurance on the face of the document, without a specific clause in the Bill, they could not as readily get further and necessary aid from the money markets.
Mr.	BORDEN:	My	hon. friendstarts,	I think,	from a premise
that is not strictly accurate. We are not taking over the control of the road; we are leaving the control and management of the road practically where it is at the present time until default comes. If default comes we must take over these roads undoubtedly, as one transcontinental system. But in the meantime the purpose of this arrangement is to get the stock of all these companies under one management, and to bring about an amalgamation so far as it is practicable at the present time. However, I am ready to consider my hon. friend's suggestion.

What I object to is that
the Government in case of default takes control, and yet does not take upon itself the specific obligation of operation and control of the road.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It takes a good deal more than control; it takes ownership.
If it likes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
You might say that of
any road in the system, but as a matter of fact all these roads form one transcontinental system and will have to be operated as such. It would be utterly impossible for this line from Montreal to the Pacific to be operated without branch lines, and even if a branch were not imme-
11 p.m. diately profitable I think any person having the slightest knowledge of railway and business affairs in this country would say that any government would be very foolish indeed to let go a branch line for that reason. All the great railways in this country construct or acquire branch lines-perhaps not so rapidly as they are sometimes desired-which are not immediately profitable, but are indirectly profitable even at first, perhaps, and in the end exceedingly profitable with the growth and development of the country. I

think my hon. friend need not have any cause for alarm in that regard. However, I will take his suggestion into consideration.

I am only bringing it up now that it may be considered when the Bill comes down.
